description: Adds the number of groups and the group size instead of multiplying them
example: 4 groups of 3 written as 4 + 3 = 7

description: Lines up the right edges of decimals instead of the decimal points
Adds to or takes from one side of an equation or balance only
example: Takes 3 from the left side of 2x + 3 = 11 and leaves the right side at 11

description: Compares lengths without a shared start line
example: Says two pencils with different starts are a fair comparison

description: Forgets to add the carried ten, hundred or thousand
Works out only one side of an equation when checking a solution, or accepts a value because it appears in the equation
example: Says x = 2 works in 3x + 5 = -1 after finding 3 x 2 + 5 = 11

description: Mixes up the coefficient, the variable and the constant of an expression, or gives 0 for a variable with no number
example: Says the coefficient of x in 8 + x is 0

description: Counts on from the smaller number, so 2 + 9 is counted from 2 and the count is lost
example: Counted on 8 from 3 and got 10 instead of starting at 8

description: Thinks the total changes when counting from the other end
example: Counts 6 from the left, then says 5 from the right

description: Counts back across a ten and lands on the wrong ten
Uses 10 as the denominator whatever the number of decimal places
Adds the whole parts and the decimal parts as separate numbers
example: 2.6 + 1.5 written as 3.11

description: Thinks no decimal fits between two neighbouring decimals
example: Says nothing is between 0.4 and 0.5

description: Uses the number of other outcomes as the denominator instead of the total
example: 2 red and 3 blue: P(red) = 2/3

description: Adds two bars when the question asks how many more
example: Girls 16, boys 10, 'how many more' answered 26

description: Joins the points of a graph with a line when the input can only be a whole number
example: Joins the points for the number of cats and their legs

description: Flips the first fraction, or neither, when dividing fractions
Divides by a fraction without turning the second fraction upside down
Moves the decimal point in the divisor only, not in the dividend
Thinks a power with the exponent 1 is 1 or 0 instead of the base
example: Writes m^1 = 1

description: Names a flat face of an object instead of the solid
example: A cereal box is a rectangle

description: Gives the basic fact with too few or too many zeros when numbers are in hundreds or thousands
Judges a game fair from the list of outcomes or a few plays rather than the probability of each player winning
example: Calls a game unfair after 7 wins in 10 plays

description: Builds equivalent fractions by adding the same number to both parts
Adds the tops and the bottoms of fractions, or multiplies by adding, instead of using a common denominator
Writes the digits of a fraction side by side as a decimal
Reads the whole ten-frame or five-frame instead of the shaded squares
example: Says 5 for a frame with 3 shaded

description: Reads a free-item offer as a percent off the whole or as a half price
example: Says 'buy 2, get 1 free' is 50% off

description: Thinks a full small container holds more than an empty big one
example: Says a full cup holds more than an empty bucket

description: Names a leg as the hypotenuse, usually the first side listed, instead of the side across from the right angle
example: Calls 9 the hypotenuse of a triangle with sides 9, 40 and 41

description: Mixes up independent and dependent events, such as drawing with and without putting the first back
example: Calls two cards drawn without replacement independent

description: Puts the output value in the input place of the rule when finding an input
example: Solves y = 3x + 2 with y = 20 by computing 3 x 20 + 2

description: Writes the value of a letter beside the number instead of operating
example: 7n with n = 5 read as 75

description: Says the counting words again instead of the last number as the total
example: Says one, two, three, four for 4 hearts

description: Thinks a decimal with more digits is bigger
example: 0.405 is bigger than 0.5

description: Counts units with gaps or overlaps as a fair measure
example: Counted 5 cubes with a gap between two of them and called it fair

description: Writes a numeral backwards or upside down, or mixes up numerals that look alike
example: Writes a backwards 3 or turns 6 into 9

description: Writes a numeral backwards or upside down
example: Wrote 9 dots as 6, or a mirror 7

description: Forgets that mean x number of values is the total when working back from a mean
example: Says 5 numbers with a mean of 6 add to 11

description: Subtracts the known side from the perimeter and forgets to halve
example: Perimeter 20, length 6: width 14

description: Thinks a shape can have only one name
example: A square is not a rectangle

description: Uses a near double but forgets the extra one or two
Changes only one side of an equation or balance, so it no longer stays equal
example: Takes 3 off the left side of x + 3 = 10 only

description: Adds the ones to the tens digit of a teen number, so 13 + 4 becomes 53
example: 13 + 4 written as 53

description: Adds when the story takes away, or takes away when the story adds
example: Says 4 balloons, 1 pops: 5 left

description: Thinks an integer is its own opposite, or writes the same sign for the opposite
example: The opposite of -7 is -7

description: Counts HT and TH (or any reordered pair) as the same outcome, so lists too few outcomes
example: Two coins: HH, HT, TT

description: Thinks an outlier changes the median as much as it changes the mean
example: Says adding 100 to 2, 3, 3, 4 changes the median a lot

description: Ignores the leftover object when pairing to decide even or odd
example: Calls 9 even after pairing leaves one over

description: Sees one pair or triple of a prime factor and decides the number is a perfect square or cube, ignoring unpaired primes
example: Says 20 = 2 x 2 x 5 is a perfect square because of the pair of 2s

description: Writes two parts side by side as one number instead of adding them
example: Writes 43 for 4 and 3

description: Writes two parts side by side as one number instead of adding them, including 10 and 6 as 106
example: 3 red and 4 blue dots written as 34; 10 + 5 written as 105

description: Does not see a pattern returns to its start after the last position
example: Dot after bottom-left said to repeat instead of going to top-left

description: Moves the decimal point the wrong number of places when changing a percent that is under 1 or over 100
example: Writes 150% as 0.15 or 0.5% as 0.5

description: Adds or subtracts percents that apply one after another, such as a discount and a tax
example: Treats 20% off then 12% tax as 8% off

description: Gives a digit's value one place too small or too large
example: The 7 in 472 315 is worth 7 000

description: Leaves a zero out of the quotient
Uses the diameter where the radius is needed, or the reverse, for a circle or cylinder
example: Uses 10 as the radius of a base with diameter 10

description: Calls every comparison a ratio, or does not see that a rate compares different units
example: Calls 90 km in 2 hours a ratio

description: Treats a part-to-part ratio as a part-to-whole fraction
example: Red to blue 3 : 2, so red is 3/2 = 150%

description: Divides all terms of a ratio by a common factor but stops before lowest terms
example: Simplifies 12:18:30 to 6:9:15

description: Regroups one whole from a mixed number but writes the wrong number of parts, or ignores the regrouped whole
Gives a remainder as large as or larger than the divisor
Leaves a remainder as big as or bigger than the divisor
Always rounds down, ignoring whether the number is closer to the next ten
example: Rounds 38 to 30

description: Uses the scale or the scale factor the wrong way round: multiplies when the drawing needs dividing or gives a reduction factor above 1
example: A 20 cm side that becomes 5 cm is called scale factor 4

description: Counts each gap or tick mark on a scaled axis as 1 instead of its value
example: Reads the 4th gap with each gap worth 5 as 4

description: Thinks a shape is a different kind when it is bigger, smaller or turned
example: Says a tilted square is not a square

description: Shares a quantity equally when the question asks to share it in a ratio
example: Shares $40 in the ratio 3:5 as $20 and $20

description: Changes the sign of only the first term when subtracting a bracket
example: (5n - 7) - (2n + 3) written as 3n - 4

description: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in each column, whichever is on top
Writes a subtraction with the smaller number first
example: 9 frogs, 2 hop away written as 2 - 9 = 7

description: Counts the symbols in a graph instead of using what each symbol stands for
example: 4 stars worth 5 each read as 4

description: Points the < or > symbol the wrong way
example: Writes 29 > 31

description: Counts a bundle of five tally marks as one
example: 3 bundles and 2 marks read as 5

description: Mixes up a teen number word with the matching tens word
example: Writes sixty as 16

description: Mixes up a teen word with the matching tens word, such as twelve and twenty
example: Matched 'twenty' to 12

description: Drops the ten when taking ones from a teen and gives only the ones left
example: 18 - 6 written as 2 instead of 12

description: Treats tenths and hundredths as the same size
example: 0.4 written as 4/100

description: Stops a factor tree at a composite number instead of splitting down to primes
example: Writes 24 = 3 x 8 as prime factors

description: Undoes the operations of a two-step equation in the wrong order
example: Divides 19 by 3 first, then subtracts 4, for 3x + 4 = 19

description: Thinks body-part units such as hands or steps measure as fairly as same-size units
example: Said steps are fair because everyone has feet

description: Mixes up the front view and the side view of a cube object, or reads one row as the whole view
example: Gives the front view of back row 1 2, front row 3 1 as 3 1 instead of 3 2

description: Calls something a need because it is liked or useful
example: Says a video game is a need

description: Picks the likely event by what the child wants, not what usually happens
example: Says a snow day in summer is likely

description: Gets subtraction with zero or the same number wrong, such as 5 - 0 = 0
example: 6 - 6 written as 6

description: Does not treat 0 as a number meaning none
example: Says 0 means 1 apple
